title: Sets, Dictionaries, and Choosing the Right One
lead:
Question Three of the last paper handed you four kinds of data and asked you
to pick the best collection for each. That question is unanswerable if you do not know the
four containers, and nearly free if you do.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Remove duplicates with a set and compare two sets to find who is in one and not the other; store and look up paired data in a dictionary; and, given a described collection of data, choose the right container for each part of it and justify the choice.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A set is a collection in curly braces with two rules: it holds no duplicates, and it has no order, so there are no indexes.
frames.ask:
The paper's attendance list is Esther, John, Mercy, Paul, Esther, John.
How many names are in the set of it?

frames.teach:
The repeats simply vanish.

attended = ["Esther", "John", "Mercy", "Paul", "Esther", "John"]
unique = set(attended)
print(len(unique))
print(sorted(unique))
4
['Esther', 'John', 'Mercy', 'Paul']

Note set(attended): passing a list to set() is the standard way to remove duplicates, and it is exactly what requirement (iii) of the question asks for.
frames.ask: Why did the program print sorted(unique) rather than just unique?

frames.check: Because a set has no order,
frames.teach:
so printing it gives
the names in an unpredictable arrangement. Sorting makes the output predictable, which
matters when the examiner is comparing your output to theirs.
frames.ask: Since a set has no order, can you write unique[0]?

frames.teach:
No order means no indexes.
Now the part that earns marks: comparing two sets. There are four operations and the paper
asks for three of them.
frames.ask:
Which students registered but did not attend? What
operation is that?

frames.check: Difference, written with a minus sign.
frames.teach:
registered = {"Esther", "John", "Paula", "Paul", "Peter", "Ada"}
attended = {"Esther", "John", "Mercy", "Paul", "Paula"}
print(sorted(registered - attended))
print(sorted(attended - registered))
print(sorted(registered & attended))
print(sorted(registered | attended))
['Ada', 'Peter']
['Mercy']
['Esther', 'John', 'Paul', 'Paula']
['Ada', 'Esther', 'John', 'Mercy', 'Paul', 'Paula', 'Peter']

Read them in order: registered minus attended is who registered but never came; attended minus registered is who turned up uninvited; & is the intersection, those in both; | is the union, everyone mentioned at all.
frames.ask:
Which one answers "students who attended but were not
registered"?

frames.teach:
The order
matters and reversing it is the commonest slip. Read the phrase from left to right and write
the sets down in the same order.
A dictionary stores pairs: a key and the value that belongs to it, written {key: value}. You look things up by key rather than by position.
frames.ask:
The paper gives Esther 60, John 55, Mercy 65, Paul 80. What is the key and
what is the value?

frames.check: The name is the key, the score is the value.
frames.teach:
scores = {"Esther": 60, "John": 55, "Mercy": 65, "Paul": 80}
print(scores["Paul"])
scores["Ada"] = 72
del scores["John"]
print(sorted(scores.keys()))
print(sorted(scores.values()))
for name, mark in sorted(scores.items()):
    print(name, mark)
80
['Ada', 'Esther', 'Mercy', 'Paul']
[60, 65, 72, 80]
Ada 72
Esther 60
Mercy 65
Paul 80

Four operations to know: look up with d[key], add or change with d[key] = value, delete with del d[key], and walk through with for k, v in d.items().
frames.ask:
What happens if you look up a key that
is not there?

frames.teach: That is the trap from Day 1's error lesson, and it is why keys are case sensitive.
frames.ask: What must a key be able to do, that a list cannot?

frames.teach:
Strings,
numbers and tuples can be keys; lists and sets cannot. Now the last requirement of the
paper's question: display every student who scored 60 and above.
frames.ask:
Which of the four containers makes that easy, and what do you loop
over?

frames.teach:
scores = {"Esther": 60, "John": 55, "Mercy": 65, "Paul": 80}
for name, mark in sorted(scores.items()):
    if mark >= 60:
        print(name, "scored", mark)
Esther scored 60
Mercy scored 65
Paul scored 80

Walk the pairs, test the value, print the ones that pass. That is the shape of every "display those which" requirement on the paper.
frames.ask:
Finally: for the workshop's fixed details, the registered names, the
duplicate free attendance and the name to score pairs, name the four containers.

frames.check: Tuple, list, set, dictionary, in that order.
frames.teach: Fixed details that must not change is a tuple; a plain roll of names in order is a list; duplicates removed is a set; a name paired with a score is a dictionary. Say the reason as well as the name: the reason is where the marks are.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The four containers, and when to choose each
blocks.html:
ContainerWrittenOrderedChangeableDuplicatesChoose it when
list[ ]yesyesalloweda sequence that may grow or change
tuple( )yesnoalloweda fixed record that must not change
set{ }noyesremoveduniqueness, or comparing two groups
dict{k: v}insertion orderyeskeys uniqueeach item is paired

The set operations, by symbol: a - b is in a but not b, a & b is in both, a | b is in either.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: how to justify a choice, in the examiner's terms
blocks.problem: Question. A program keeps four things: the registered students, one workshop's details (title, room, day, capacity), the attendance with no repeats, and each student's score. Name the most suitable Python collection for each, and give the reason in one sentence. The paper wants the name AND the reason; the reason is what separates full marks from half.
blocks.working:
When the paper asks for "the most suitable Python collection", it wants the name AND the reason. One sentence each is enough, and it is what separates full marks from half.

  • Registered students: a list. The names are a simple ordered sequence that may be added to, and duplicates in the raw register are meaningful data.
  • Workshop details: a tuple. The title, room, day and capacity form one fixed record that should not be altered once set, and a tuple enforces that.
  • Duplicate free attendance: a set. A set discards repeats automatically, and it supports the comparisons needed to find who registered but did not attend.
  • Student scores: a dictionary. Each score belongs to a named student, so the data is naturally key to value, and the score can be found by name without searching.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Reversing a set difference. "Registered but did not attend" is registered - attended, in that order.
  • Indexing a set. There is no order, so s[0] is an error.
  • {} alone is an empty dictionary, not an empty set. For an empty set you must write set().
  • Printing a set and expecting a fixed order. Wrap it in sorted().

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What does len(set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])) give?

2. Write the expression for members of a who are not in b.

3. Why can a list not be a dictionary key?

4. Which container for: a fixed exam date; a register of names; the unique subjects offered; each student's matric number?
blocks.answer: 1. 3. 2. a - b. 3. Because a list is mutable and therefore not hashable; a key must have a stable hash. 4. Tuple, list, set, dictionary.

blocks.big:
List grows, tuple is fixed, set is unique, dictionary pairs. Name the
container and give the reason: the reason carries the mark.
blocks.sub: Registered minus attended, in that order. Read the phrase left to right and write the sets in the same order.

title: Functions: Void and Value Returning
lead: Functions carried Question Three and Question Six on the last paper, and part of Question Four. That is nearly forty marks available to someone who can write def and return without hesitating.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Define a function, call it and assign what it gives back; state the difference between a void and a value returning function with an example of each; distinguish built in from user defined; list five benefits of modularising with functions; and write a program the paper's way, where a named function does the displaying.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach:
A function is a named block of code you write once and use as often as you like. You define it with def, and nothing inside it happens until you call it by name. 

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)
    print("Welcome to CSC241")

greet("Esther")
greet("John")
frames.ask:
In the program below, how many lines of output
are there, and why?

frames.teach:
because the body has two prints and it is called twice.

Hello, Esther
Welcome to CSC241
Hello, John
Welcome to CSC241

The word in the brackets of the definition, name, is the parameter; the value you pass in when you call it, "Esther", is the argument.
frames.ask:
That function prints but hands nothing back. What is the
name for that kind?

frames.teach:
The other kind uses return to hand a value back to whoever called it, and that is a value returning function. 

def cube(num):
    return num * num * num

result = cube(4)
print(result)
print(cube(2) + cube(3))
frames.ask: Read the paper's own cube function. Write the statement that passes 4 to it and puts the answer in result.

frames.teach:
64
35

Because it returns a value, a call to it can be used anywhere a value can be used, which is why cube(2) + cube(3) works.
frames.ask: Could you write greet("Ada") + 1 with the void function from before?

frames.teach:
A void function returns the special value None, and you cannot do arithmetic with it. Here is the difference made visible.

def show(n):
    print("the number is", n)

def double(n):
    return n * 2

a = show(5)
b = double(5)
print("show returned:", a)
print("double returned:", b)
the number is 5
show returned: None
double returned: 10
frames.ask: So what is the single sentence that distinguishes the two?

frames.teach: Learn that sentence, it is worth marks on its own.

A function can take several parameters, and a parameter can have a default so the caller may leave it out. You can also pass arguments by name, in any order. 

def total_cost(price, quantity, discount=0):
    return price * quantity - discount

print(total_cost(100, 3))
print(total_cost(100, 3, 50))
print(total_cost(quantity=2, price=250))
frames.ask:
Read the three calls below and predict the three
answers.

frames.teach:
300
250
500

The first call takes the default discount of 0. The second supplies 50. The third names its arguments, so their order does not matter.
frames.ask: Can a function return more than one value?

frames.teach:
and you unpack them into several names on the left.

def get_data():
    radius = 12
    price = 20
    labour = 1500
    return radius, price, labour

r, p, lab = get_data()
print(r, p, lab)
12 20 1500

That is exactly what the paper's get_data() is asked to do.
frames.ask:
Now a subtle one. If a function assigns to a name that also exists outside
it, does the outside one change?

frames.teach:
total = 0

def add_ten():
    total = 10
    print("inside the function:", total)

add_ten()
print("outside the function:", total)
inside the function: 10
outside the function: 0

A name created inside a function is local to it and disappears when the function ends. That is called scope, and it is precisely why functions are safe to reuse.
frames.ask: Now the paper's Question Six shape. It insists the report is displayed by a void function called display_achievement_summary. Is displaying the right job for a void function?

frames.check: Yes: it acts, it does not compute a value.
frames.teach:
Here is the whole program, exactly the shape the requirements ask for.

def display_achievement_summary(user_name, actual_total,
                                target_total):
    print("--- Progress Report for", user_name, "---")
    print("Total Steps:", actual_total)
    if actual_total >= target_total:
        print("Milestone Achieved!")
    else:
        print("Milestone Not Achieved.")

name = input("Enter your name: ")
days = int(input("Enter the number of days to track: "))
goal = int(input("Enter your daily step goal: "))

total_steps = 0
for day in range(1, days + 1):
    steps = int(input(f"Enter steps for day {day}: "))
    total_steps += steps

target = goal * days
display_achievement_summary(name, total_steps, target)
Enter your name: Alice
Enter the number of days to track: 3
Enter your daily step goal: 10000
Enter steps for day 1: 12000
Enter steps for day 2: 9000
Enter steps for day 3: 11000
--- Progress Report for Alice ---
Total Steps: 32000
Milestone Achieved!

Read the structure, because it is the template for every "use a function" question: read the inputs, loop to accumulate, work out the target, then call the named function with exactly the arguments the paper listed.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Five benefits, and the four distinctions
blocks.html:
Five benefits of modularising a program with functions, which the paper asks for by name:

  • Reusability. Write the code once and call it from as many places as you need.
  • Readability. A well named call says what is happening; the detail is elsewhere.
  • Easier debugging and testing. A fault is isolated inside one small block that can be tested on its own.
  • Easier maintenance. A change is made in one place and takes effect everywhere.
  • Teamwork and simpler design. A large problem is broken into smaller independent pieces that different people can write separately.
PairThe differenceExample
Built in vs user definedbuilt in comes with Python and needs no definition; user defined is one you write with deflen() against cube()
Void vs value returningvoid performs an action and returns None; value returning computes a result and hands it backprint() against len()
Parameter vs argumentthe parameter is the name in the definition; the argument is the value supplied at the calldef cube(num) against cube(4)
Local vs globala name made inside a function exists only theresee the scope listing above

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Printing instead of returning. If the question says the function returns the area, print(area) earns nothing. return area is the answer.
  • Defining but never calling. A definition on its own produces no output at all.
  • Using the function's exact name. When the paper names the function, use that name and those parameters, spelled exactly as printed. It is a mark.
  • x = print("hi") puts None into x.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Write the statement that passes 4 to cube and stores the answer in result. What is in result?

2. In one sentence each, define a void and a value returning function.

3. What does a void function actually return?

4. On paper, write a value returning function area(r) that uses math.pi.
blocks.answer: 1. result = cube(4), and result holds 64. 2. A void function performs an action and returns no value; a value returning function computes and hands back a result with return. 3. None. 4. import math then def area(r): and return math.pi * r ** 2.

blocks.big:
def defines it, the call runs it, return hands something back. No return means
None.
blocks.sub: If the paper names the function and its parameters, copy that name and those parameters exactly. The examiner is looking for them.

title: Modules, and Importing What You Need
lead:
A short lesson, but Question Six of the last paper said the value of pi
"should be obtained from the math module", which is a direct instruction worth a mark. Miss
the import and you lose it.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Say what a module is and why programs use them; import one in both of the two ways and know which names each way gives you; and use math.pi in a calculation the paper asks for.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A module is simply a Python file full of ready made functions and values that somebody else has written and tested. Using one saves you writing it and saves you getting it wrong.
frames.ask:
Name any module you have already heard
of.

frames.teach:
To use a module you must first import it. The plain form gives you the module's name, and you then reach inside it with a dot. 

import math

print(math.pi)
print(math.sqrt(16))
print(math.ceil(4.1))
print(math.floor(4.9))
print(round(math.pi, 2))
frames.ask: Read the program and say what math.pi gives.

frames.teach:
3.141592653589793
4.0
5
4
3.14

Note the difference between math.ceil(), which always rounds up to the next whole number, math.floor(), which always rounds down, and plain round(), which goes to the nearest and takes a number of decimal places.
frames.ask: After import math, can you write pi on its own?

frames.teach:
The import gave you the module, not the names inside it. The second form of import takes named things out of the module and puts them straight into your program.

from math import pi, sqrt

print(pi)
print(sqrt(25))
3.141592653589793
5.0
frames.ask: So with from math import pi, do you write math.pi or pi?

frames.teach: and writing math.pi would now be an error, because the name math was never imported. Choose one form and stay with it.
frames.ask: Which form makes it clearer to a reader where a name came from?

frames.teach:
because every use is labelled. That is the form to prefer in the exam. One more you may meet.

import random

random.seed(1)
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["a", "b", "c"]))
2
c

Two functions worth knowing there: random.randint(a, b) gives a whole number from a to b inclusive, and random.choice(seq) picks one item from a list at random. The seed line is only there so this book prints the same numbers every time; you would not normally write it.
frames.ask: Now the paper's own question. Write the first line of a program that must compute the area of a circle using math.pi.

frames.teach:
Here is the whole flooring estimate from Question Six part (c), built from three value returning functions exactly as the requirements list them.

import math

def get_data():
    radius = float(input("Enter room radius (meters): "))
    price = float(input("Enter flooring price per square meter: "))
    labour = float(input("Enter labor fee: "))
    return radius, price, labour

def calculate_area(radius):
    return math.pi * radius ** 2

def calculate_total(area, material_price, labor_fee):
    return area * material_price + labor_fee

r, price, labour = get_data()
area = calculate_area(r)
total = calculate_total(area, price, labour)

print("--- Project Estimate ---")
print(f"Total Calculated Cost: {total:.2f}")
if total > 10000:
    print("Status: Requires Senior Management Approval.")
else:
    print("Status: Senior Management Approval is not required.")
Enter room radius (meters): 12
Enter flooring price per square meter: 20
Enter labor fee: 1500
--- Project Estimate ---
Total Calculated Cost: 10547.79
Status: Requires Senior Management Approval.

Read the total carefully: 10547.79. The paper's own sample interaction prints 10546.90 for the same inputs, and the paper is wrong: with math.pi the answer is 10547.79. Use math.pi as instructed, show your working, and do not try to reproduce their arithmetic slip.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The two imports, and what each gives you
blocks.html:
WrittenWhat you getHow you use it
import maththe module itselfmath.pi, math.sqrt(16)
from math import pijust that namepi, on its own
from math import *every name in itworks, but hides where names came from
import math as mthe module, renamedm.pi

Why modules exist, in the words the paper wants: a module is a file containing Python definitions and statements that can be imported and reused by other programs. Modules give reusability, keep programs shorter and easier to read, group related work in one place, and let you use large amounts of reliable, already tested code without rewriting it.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Using math.pi after from math import pi. That is a NameError. The two forms are not interchangeable.
  • Using 3.14 when the paper says to use the math module. It is an explicit instruction and a mark.
  • Putting the import inside a function. It works, but the import belongs at the top of the program, and the examiner expects to see it there.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What is a module, in one sentence?

2. After import math, how do you write the square root of 81?

3. What is the difference between math.floor(4.9) and round(4.9)?

4. Write the two lines that import math and print pi to two decimal places.
blocks.answer: 1. A file of Python definitions and statements that other programs can import and reuse. 2. math.sqrt(81). 3. floor always goes down, giving 4; round goes to nearest, giving 5. 4. import math then print(round(math.pi, 2)).

blocks.big:
import math gives you math dot something. from math import pi gives you pi
alone. Never mix the two.
blocks.sub: When the paper names the module, import it in your answer. The instruction is the mark.

title: File Handling
lead:
Question Five of the last paper was file handling from top to bottom, all
seventeen and a half marks of it, and three of its four parts were short theory. It is one
of the most answerable questions on the paper.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Say what file handling is; list and explain four access modes of open(); state the difference between reading and appending; and write a program that creates a text file, adds more records to it later without destroying the first ones, and reads them all back, or just the first five.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Everything a program holds in variables disappears the moment it stops. File handling is the business of writing data to a file on disk so it survives, and reading it back later.
frames.ask:
What three steps must every file operation
have?

frames.check: Open the file, work with it, close it.
frames.teach:
You open with open(filename, mode), which hands back a file object, and the mode is a single letter that says what you intend to do. 

f = open("students.txt", "w")
f.write("Name: John Doe, Score: 78\n")
f.write("Name: Mary James, Score: 85\n")
f.close()

print(open("students.txt").read())
frames.ask:
Read the program
below. Which letter did it use to create the file?

frames.teach:
Name: John Doe, Score: 78
Name: Mary James, Score: 85

The \n at the end of each written string is the newline: without it every record would run into the next on one long line. write() does not add one for you.
frames.ask: What do you think happens if you open an existing file with "w" a second time?

frames.check: Everything already in it is destroyed.
frames.teach:
This is the single most important fact in the lesson, and the paper tests it directly.

f = open("notes.txt", "w")
f.write("the original line\n")
f.close()

f = open("notes.txt", "w")
f.write("the second line\n")
f.close()

print(open("notes.txt").read())
the second line

The original line is gone.
frames.ask:
So which mode adds to a file without
destroying what is there?

frames.teach:
It opens the file with the position at the very end, so everything you write goes after the existing content. That is exactly requirement (ii) of the paper's question.

f = open("students.txt", "w")
f.write("Name: John Doe, Score: 78\n")
f.close()

f = open("students.txt", "a")
f.write("Name: Mary James, Score: 85\n")
f.close()

print(open("students.txt").read())
Name: John Doe, Score: 78
Name: Mary James, Score: 85
frames.ask:
State, in one sentence each, the difference between reading and
appending.

frames.teach: Reading uses "r" and fails if the file does not exist; appending uses "a" and creates the file if it does not exist.

There are three ways to read, and choosing the right one is what the
marks are on.
frames.ask:
Which one would you use to get the file back as a list, one
item per line?

frames.teach:
f = open("data.txt", "w")
f.write("alpha\nbeta\ngamma\ndelta\n")
f.close()

f = open("data.txt", "r")
print("read():", repr(f.read()))
f.close()

f = open("data.txt", "r")
print("readline():", repr(f.readline()))
f.close()

f = open("data.txt", "r")
print("readlines():", f.readlines())
f.close()
read(): 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\ndelta\n'
readline(): 'alpha\n'
readlines(): ['alpha\n', 'beta\n', 'gamma\n', 'delta\n']

read() gives the whole file as one string, readline() gives the next single line, and readlines() gives a list of all the lines, each still carrying its newline. The listing wraps the first two in repr(), which shows a value the way Python would write it, quotes and newline markers included, so you can actually see the line endings that a plain print would hide.
frames.ask: Given a list of lines, how would you print only the first five?

frames.teach:
That is requirement (iv) of the paper's question, and it is a one line answer if you thought of readlines().

with open("records.txt", "w") as f:
    for i in range(1, 8):
        f.write(f"Student {i}, Score: {60 + i}\n")

with open("records.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print("All records:", len(lines))
print("The first five:")
for line in lines[:5]:
    print(line.strip())
All records: 7
The first five:
Student 1, Score: 61
Student 2, Score: 62
Student 3, Score: 63
Student 4, Score: 64
Student 5, Score: 65

Note line.strip() in the print, which removes the newline the file kept.
frames.ask: What would the output look like without the strip?

frames.teach: because each line would carry its own newline and print would add another. Finally, the tidier way to open a file.
frames.ask: What is the risk of writing close() yourself?

frames.check:
Forgetting it, or never reaching it because the program
failed first.
frames.teach:
with closes the file for you, automatically, whatever happens.

with open("scores.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Esther 60\n")
    f.write("John 55\n")

with open("scores.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, mark = line.split()
        print(name, "scored", mark)
Esther scored 60
John scored 55

Read the shape: with open(...) as f: then an indented block. Notice also for line in f:, which walks a file line by line without loading it all, and line.split() cutting each record into its fields.
frames.ask: Which style should you use in the exam?

frames.teach: with is better practice and shorter; open and close is what most course material shows. Use whichever you can write correctly under pressure, but if you use open, never forget the close().

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The four modes the paper asks for
blocks.html:
Question Five part (b) asks you to list and explain four file access modes, for six marks. These four, with these explanations.

ModeNameWhat it doesIf the file does not exist
"r"readopens for reading only, position at the start; the file cannot be changedraises FileNotFoundError
"w"writeopens for writing and erases everything already in the filecreates it
"a"appendopens for writing with the position at the end, so new data is added and existing data is keptcreates it
"r+"read and writeopens for both reading and writing, position at the start, without truncatingraises FileNotFoundError

The definition to learn: file handling is the process of creating, opening, reading, writing and closing files on secondary storage so that data persists after the program has finished running.

The three reads: read() whole file as one string, readline() one line, readlines() a list of every line.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Using "w" for the append step. Requirement (ii) says append without deleting the existing records; "w" deletes them all and loses the marks for both parts.
  • Forgetting the \n. Without it every record joins the last one.
  • Forgetting close(). Data can still be sitting in a buffer, unwritten.
  • Reopening a different filename. The paper insists the file created at the start is used for every later operation, so use the same name throughout, ideally stored in a variable.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Which mode adds to a file without destroying it, and which one destroys it?

2. What does readlines() return, and what does each item still carry?

3. Write the line that prints only the first five records from a list called lines.

4. In one sentence, the difference between reading and appending.
blocks.answer: 1. "a" appends, "w" truncates. 2. A list of all the lines, each still ending with its newline character. 3. for line in lines[:5]: print(line.strip()). 4. Reading takes data out and leaves the file unchanged; appending adds new data at the end and keeps everything already there.

blocks.big:
w wipes, a adds, r reads. Open, work, close, and always write the newline
yourself.
blocks.sub: The paper's whole file question turns on one letter. If it says append, the mode is a.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: Exception Handling
lead:
No part of the last paper was purely about exceptions, but the objective
section tests them and every "validate the input" requirement is better answered with them.
It is a short lesson that makes your long answers look professional.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Say what an exception is and how it differs from a syntax error; name the common exception types and what causes each; and wrap risky work in try and except so a bad input produces a polite message instead of a crash.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: There are two kinds of thing that go wrong. A syntax error is bad grammar: Python cannot even read the program, so nothing runs at all. An exception is a fault that happens while the program is running, when the code is perfectly legal but the situation is impossible.
frames.ask:
Which kind is dividing by a number that
happens to be zero?

frames.teach: because a / b is perfectly good Python and only fails when b turns out to be 0. An unhandled exception stops the program dead and prints a traceback.
frames.ask: Given int("not a number"), what do you think the exception is called?

frames.teach:
the type is right, a string, but the value cannot be made into a number.

try:
    n = int("not a number")
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a whole number.")
That was not a whole number.

The shape is try: with the risky work indented under it, then except SomeError: with what to do about it.
frames.ask: If the try block succeeds, does the except block run?

frames.teach:
The except runs only when that exception actually happens. Here are the five you must recognise on sight.

for job in ["zero", "type", "value", "key", "file"]:
    try:
        if job == "zero":
            10 / 0
        elif job == "type":
            "2" + 2
        elif job == "value":
            int("abc")
        elif job == "key":
            {"a": 1}["b"]
        else:
            open("no_such_file.txt")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{job:6s} -> {type(e).__name__}")
zero   -> ZeroDivisionError
type   -> TypeError
value  -> ValueError
key    -> KeyError
file   -> FileNotFoundError
frames.ask: Which one would you catch around int(input(...))?

frames.teach: because that is what a non numeric answer raises. There are two optional extra blocks. else runs when the try succeeded, and finally runs every time, whether it worked or not.
frames.ask: What is finally for, in practice?

frames.check: Cleaning up, such as closing a file,
frames.teach:
because it runs even when something went wrong.

def read_score(text):
    try:
        score = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        print("Invalid input, please enter a number.")
        return None
    else:
        print("Accepted:", score)
        return score
    finally:
        print("(the finally block always runs)")

read_score("75")
read_score("seventy")
Accepted: 75
(the finally block always runs)
Invalid input, please enter a number.
(the finally block always runs)
frames.ask: Look at the second call. Which lines ran, and in what order?

frames.check: The except block, then the finally.
frames.teach: The else was skipped because the try did not succeed.
frames.ask:
Now put it to work: validate a score that must be a number between 0 and
100.

frames.check: Catch the bad type with except and the bad range with an if.
frames.teach:
values = ["85", "abc", "120"]
for text in values:
    try:
        score = int(text)
        if score < 0 or score > 100:
            print(text, "-> out of range")
        else:
            print(text, "-> accepted")
    except ValueError:
        print(text, "-> not a number")
85 -> accepted
abc -> not a number
120 -> out of range

That is the pattern to use in any question that says "validate": try to convert, except to catch nonsense, if to check the range. It answers the requirement more fully than an if alone, because an if alone still crashes on abc.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The exceptions, and the block order
blocks.html:
ExceptionRaised whenExample
ValueErrorright type, impossible valueint("abc")
TypeErrorwrong type for the operation"2" + 2
ZeroDivisionErrordivide or modulus by zero10 / 0
KeyErrordictionary key not presentd["missing"]
IndexErrorindex past the end of a sequence[1, 2][5]
FileNotFoundErroropening a file that is not there for readingopen("gone.txt")
NameErrorusing a name never definedprint(mystring)

The full shape, in order: try the risky work, except each fault you can handle, else for what to do when nothing went wrong, finally for the cleanup that must happen either way.

The definition: an exception is an error detected during execution which interrupts the normal flow of the program; exception handling is the use of try and except to catch it and respond gracefully rather than let the program terminate.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Catching everything with a bare except:. It hides real bugs, including your own typing mistakes. Name the exception you expect.
  • Putting the whole program inside one try. Then you cannot tell which line failed. Wrap only the risky line.
  • Confusing a syntax error with an exception. A syntax error stops the program from running at all and cannot be caught by try.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What is the difference between a syntax error and an exception?

2. Which exception does int("twelve") raise?

3. When does a finally block run?

4. Write the three lines that safely read a whole number from the user.
blocks.answer: 1. A syntax error is bad grammar found before the program runs, so nothing runs; an exception happens during running, in legal code, and can be caught. 2. ValueError. 3. Always, whether the try succeeded or failed. 4. try: then n = int(input("Number: ")) then except ValueError: print("Please enter a number.").

blocks.big:
Syntax errors stop it starting. Exceptions stop it finishing. try and except
turn a crash into a message.
blocks.sub: Whenever a question says validate, reach for try, except, then a range check. It is the fuller answer.

title: Databases: SQLite Through Python
lead:
Question Four part (c) of the last paper was this and nothing else, for ten
and a half marks, the single largest part on the whole paper. It is also the most learnable,
because it is one fixed program with the details changed.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a complete program that connects to an SQLite database, creates a table if it does not already exist, inserts a set of given records, selects all of them and a filtered subset, computes a count, a maximum and an average, updates one row and deletes another, committing as it goes.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A database keeps data in tables of rows and columns, and you speak to it in a language called SQL, structured query language. Python talks to an SQLite database through the sqlite3 module, which is built in and needs no installation.
frames.ask:
What must the first line of the program therefore
be?

frames.teach: Then three things happen in a fixed order, every single time. You connect to the database file, which creates it if it is not there; you make a cursor, which is the object that carries your commands and collects the answers; and at the end you close the connection.
frames.ask: What do you think sqlite3.connect("school.db") does if school.db does not exist yet?

frames.teach:
So one line satisfies the requirement to create the database. Now the table. Write it with IF NOT EXISTS, so running the program twice does not fail.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cur = conn.cursor()

cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS student (
                   StudentID INTEGER,
                   StudentName TEXT,
                   Class TEXT,
                   Score REAL)""")
conn.commit()
print("database and table ready")
conn.close()
database and table ready

Note the column types the paper specified: INTEGER, TEXT, TEXT, REAL.
frames.ask:
Why is Score a REAL rather than an
INTEGER?

frames.check: Because a score may have a decimal part.
frames.teach: REAL is SQL's floating point type.
frames.ask: What is conn.commit() for?

frames.teach: Until you commit, your inserts and updates are only pending and are lost when the program ends. Forgetting commit is the commonest way to lose marks on this question, because the program appears to run perfectly and the database ends up empty.
frames.ask:
Now the five records. Do
you write five separate INSERT statements?

frames.check: You can, but there is a much better way.
frames.teach:
executemany takes a list of tuples and inserts them all.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS student (
                   StudentID INTEGER, StudentName TEXT,
                   Class TEXT, Score REAL)""")

records = [(101, "David James", "SS1", 78),
           (102, "Mary Johnson", "SS2", 85),
           (103, "Peter Okoro", "SS1", 67),
           (104, "Grace Bello", "SS3", 92),
           (105, "Esther Ade", "SS2", 74)]
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", records)
conn.commit()

cur.execute("SELECT * FROM student")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)
conn.close()
(101, 'David James', 'SS1', 78.0)
(102, 'Mary Johnson', 'SS2', 85.0)
(103, 'Peter Okoro', 'SS1', 67.0)
(104, 'Grace Bello', 'SS3', 92.0)
(105, 'Esther Ade', 'SS2', 74.0)

The question marks are placeholders: SQLite fills them in from the tuple, in order.
frames.ask: Why not just build the SQL string with the values glued into it?

frames.check:
Because placeholders are safer and handle quoting for
you.
frames.teach:
A name containing an apostrophe would break a glued together string. Use
placeholders always.
To get data back you execute a SELECT and then collect the answers from the cursor. fetchall() gives every matching row as a list of tuples; fetchone() gives just the next one.
frames.ask: Which would you use for "display all student records"?

frames.check: fetchall(), then a for loop to print each row.
frames.teach: To narrow it down, add a WHERE clause, again with a placeholder.
frames.ask: Write the SELECT that returns only the SS2 students.

frames.teach:
Note the comma inside the brackets: it must be a tuple,
and a one item tuple needs that comma.
frames.ask:
Now the statistics. Which SQL
functions give a count, a highest and an average?

frames.teach: You can ask for all three in one query, and collect them with fetchone() because they come back as a single row.
frames.ask: Finally, which two statements change existing data?

frames.check: UPDATE and DELETE, and both need a WHERE.
frames.teach:
Here is the whole thing, every requirement of the paper's question in order.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS student (
                   StudentID INTEGER, StudentName TEXT,
                   Class TEXT, Score REAL)""")

records = [(101, "David James", "SS1", 78),
           (102, "Mary Johnson", "SS2", 85),
           (103, "Peter Okoro", "SS1", 67),
           (104, "Grace Bello", "SS3", 92),
           (105, "Esther Ade", "SS2", 74)]
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", records)
conn.commit()

print("Students in SS2:")
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM student WHERE Class = ?", ("SS2",))
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(" ", row)

cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(Score), AVG(Score) FROM student")
count, highest, average = cur.fetchone()
print("Total students:", count)
print("Highest score:", highest)
print("Average score:", round(average, 2))

cur.execute("UPDATE student SET Score = ? WHERE StudentName = ?",
            (75, "Peter Okoro"))
cur.execute("DELETE FROM student WHERE StudentID = ?", (105,))
conn.commit()

print("After the update and the delete:")
cur.execute("SELECT StudentID, StudentName, Score FROM student")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(" ", row)
conn.close()
Students in SS2:
  (102, 'Mary Johnson', 'SS2', 85.0)
  (105, 'Esther Ade', 'SS2', 74.0)
Total students: 5
Highest score: 92.0
Average score: 79.2
After the update and the delete:
  (101, 'David James', 78.0)
  (102, 'Mary Johnson', 85.0)
  (103, 'Peter Okoro', 75.0)
  (104, 'Grace Bello', 92.0)

Read it once more against the requirements: create, insert, select all, select SS2, statistics, update Peter Okoro, delete 105.
frames.ask: What would happen to the UPDATE if you left off the WHERE?

frames.check: Every single row would be changed.
frames.teach:
A DELETE with
no WHERE empties the table. Always write the WHERE first, then go back and write the rest of
the statement.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The seven line skeleton, and the SQL
blocks.html:
Learn this skeleton by heart. Every database question is this, with the table and the columns changed.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("name.db")      # 1 connect, creates the file
cur = conn.cursor()                    # 2 cursor carries the commands
cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ...""")   # 3
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?)", rows)  # 4
conn.commit()                          # 5 SAVE, or nothing is kept
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t")         # 6 ask
for row in cur.fetchall():             #   collect
    print(row)
conn.close()                           # 7 close
SQLDoes
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t (col TYPE, ...)makes the table, and does not fail if it is already there
INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)adds a row, values supplied as a tuple
SELECT * FROM tevery column of every row
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col = ?only the rows that match
SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(c), AVG(c) FROM thow many, highest, average
UPDATE t SET col = ? WHERE col = ?changes matching rows
DELETE FROM t WHERE col = ?removes matching rows

The four SQL types: INTEGER, TEXT, REAL, BLOB.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Forgetting conn.commit(). The program runs, prints nothing wrong, and saves nothing. This is the big one.
  • Leaving off the WHERE in an UPDATE or DELETE. It changes or removes every row.
  • A one item tuple without its comma. ("SS2") is a string; ("SS2",) is a tuple, and the placeholder needs the tuple.
  • CREATE TABLE without IF NOT EXISTS. The program then fails the second time it is run, and the paper explicitly asks for "if they do not already exist".

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Name the three objects or calls in order at the start of every database program.

2. What is lost if you forget commit()?

3. Write the SELECT that returns only students whose Score is above 70.

4. On paper, write the whole skeleton from import to close, from memory.
blocks.answer: 1. import sqlite3, sqlite3.connect(...), conn.cursor(). 2. Every insert, update and delete since the last commit; the database keeps none of it. 3. cur.execute("SELECT * FROM student WHERE Score > ?", (70,)). 4. Connect, cursor, create, insert, commit, select and fetch, close.

blocks.big:
Connect, cursor, create, insert, COMMIT, select, close. Seven steps, always
the same, and the fifth is the one everybody forgets.
blocks.sub: Ten and a half marks on the last paper for one program you can learn as a shape. Write it out from memory tonight and again tomorrow.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: A Window on the Screen, in Brief
lead:
Be honest about the weighting here. The written paper has not asked you to
build a window, but the objective section does ask about it, and this is the last twelve
objective questions of Day 3. Half an hour, recognition level, then move on.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Say what a graphical user interface is and which module Python uses for one; name the common widgets and what each is for; describe the three geometry managers; and write the six line skeleton of a window with a label, an entry and a button.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Everything you have written so far talks to the user through input and print, in a text window. A graphical user interface talks through windows, buttons, boxes and menus that the user clicks.
frames.ask: What is the standard module Python uses to build one?

frames.teach: which comes with Python and is a wrapper around a long established toolkit called Tk. The building blocks are called widgets.
frames.ask:
Guess the widget you would use to display a piece of text
the user cannot edit.

frames.teach: The six you need to recognise are Label for text, Entry for a single line the user can type in, Button for something to click, Text for several lines of typing, Frame for grouping other widgets, and Checkbutton or Radiobutton for choices.
frames.ask:
Which one collects a typed
answer?

frames.teach:
Every program has the same skeleton. You make the main window, add widgets to it, arrange them, then start the event loop, which is the line that waits for the user to do something.

import tkinter as tk

window = tk.Tk()                          # 1 the main window
window.title("Student Record")          # 2 its caption

label = tk.Label(window, text="Name:")   # 3 a widget
entry = tk.Entry(window)
button = tk.Button(window, text="Save")

label.pack()                              # 4 arrange them
entry.pack()
button.pack()

window.mainloop()                         # 5 wait for the user
frames.ask: Which line keeps the window on the screen?

frames.teach:
Without it the
program builds the window, reaches the end and exits, and the window flashes and vanishes.
That is a favourite objective question.
frames.ask: The pack() calls arrange the widgets. Can you name the other two ways?

frames.teach: These three are the geometry managers: pack stacks widgets in the order you add them, grid puts them in numbered rows and columns, and place positions them at exact pixel coordinates.
frames.ask: Which would you choose for a form of labels beside entry boxes?

frames.teach: because a form is rows and columns. And one rule worth a mark: never mix pack and grid in the same container; the program freezes.
frames.ask:
Last one. How does a button
know what to do when it is clicked?

frames.teach: which you give the name of a function, without brackets: tk.Button(window, text="Save", command=save_record). Writing command=save_record() with brackets calls it immediately instead of on the click, which is the classic mistake.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Widgets, managers, and the two rules
blocks.html:
WidgetWhat it is for
Labeldisplays text or an image the user cannot edit
Entrya single line box for the user to type in
Buttonsomething to click, which runs the function named in command
Texta multi line typing area
Framea container that groups other widgets
Checkbutton and Radiobuttonchoices: many, or one of several
Listboxa list of items to select from
Geometry managerArranges by
pack()stacking in the order added, top to bottom or side by side
grid()row and column numbers, best for forms
place()exact x and y coordinates

The definition: a graphical user interface is a visual way for a user to interact with a program through windows and controls such as buttons, labels and text boxes, rather than by typing at a text prompt. In Python the standard library module for building one is tkinter.

Two rules: the program ends without mainloop(); and never mix pack with grid inside the same container.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Which module is Python's standard toolkit for a graphical interface?

2. What does mainloop() do, and what happens without it?

3. Name the three geometry managers.

4. What is wrong with command=save() on a Button?
blocks.answer: 1. tkinter. 2. It starts the event loop and waits for the user; without it the program finishes immediately and the window disappears. 3. pack, grid and place. 4. The brackets call the function straight away; the button needs the function's name without brackets.

blocks.big:
Tk makes the window, widgets fill it, a geometry manager arranges it, and
mainloop keeps it alive.
blocks.sub: This is a recognition topic. Know the widgets, the three managers and the two rules, then spend your time on the database.

lead: Every question on this paper, printed exactly as the examiner set it. For each one: read it, write your full answer in your book, and only then open the model answer. Reading an answer you have not attempted teaches you almost nothing.

The 2024/2025 paper was rigid: every question was five parts, each worth exactly 3.5 marks, and each question sat on one module. This paper breaks all three, and a student running on the old habits misreads it.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: Briefly describe how the and operator works in Python (use examples) [2.5 marks]

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
What I am given

Nothing but the operator name. This is a bookwork part: no data, no program, just describe and show.

What is actually asked

Two things joined by "(use examples)". A description with no example cannot score full marks, and an example with no description cannot either. Answer both halves explicitly.

What the marks say

2.5 marks is the smallest part on the paper. A truth table plus one worked line is the right size. Do not write an essay here and run out of time on the 10.5-mark database question.

Where it is taught

Module Two, Unit 3 (Operators).

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to 2025/2026 paper, Question One (a) in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Answer · Q1 (a) the and operator, 2.5 marks

and is a boolean operator. It joins two conditions and is true only when both are true. If either side is false, the whole thing is false.

LeftRightleft and right
TrueTrueTrue
TrueFalseFalse
FalseTrueFalse
FalseFalseFalse

The example the marker wants is a range check:

>>> score = 72
>>> score >= 0 and score <= 100
True

Both sides hold, so the score is valid. Change score to 150 and the right side fails, so the whole test is False. and also short-circuits: if the left is false, Python never even looks at the right, because the answer is already settled.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: What is a string in Python? List and briefly explain four common string methods used in Python. Provide an example for each method. [5 marks]

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
What is actually asked

Three instructions in one part: define, list and explain four, and give an example for each. That is nine separate things to write.

What the marks say

5 marks over roughly nine items means each is worth about half a mark. Short and correct beats long and vague. A table is the fastest way to earn all of them.

The trap

It says four. Writing six wastes time and earns nothing extra; writing three throws marks away. Count what you wrote.

Where it is taught

Module Two, Unit 4 (Working with Strings).

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to 2025/2026 paper, Question One (b) in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Answer · Q1 (b) strings and four methods, 5 marks

A string is an ordered sequence of characters, written in quotes. It is immutable: its characters cannot be changed in place. Four common methods, one example each:

MethodDoesExampleGives
upper()Capitals"hi".upper()'HI'
lower()Lower case"Hi".lower()'hi'
strip()Trims ends" hi ".strip()'hi'
replace(a,b)Swaps text"hi".replace("i","o")'ho'

Each returns a new string, because the original cannot change. Others you know and could name instead: split(), count(), find(), title(). See Module Two, Unit Four for all of them.

blocks.printed:
Identify the Errors in the following code segment [3 marks]

1  person = { "name": 'John Doe', 'age': 30, 'city':
2      'New York', 'Email': 'john.doe@example.com' }
3
4  print("Name:", person['Name'])
5  print("Age:", person['Age'])
6  print("City:", person['City'])

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
What is actually asked

Identify only. It does not ask you to rewrite the code, unlike Question Two (c), which does. Listing the faults earns the marks here; a full corrected listing earns no more.

What I am given

A dictionary whose keys are 'name', 'age', 'city' and 'Email', then six accesses to it.

Where the trap sits

Every fault is the same fault: a dictionary key is case sensitive. Do not hunt for a syntax error, there is none. The line that raises nothing at all is the most dangerous one on the page.

What the marks say

3 marks and there are more than three faults, so name them in groups rather than one line at a time.

Where it is taught

Module Three, Unit 4 (Sets and Dictionaries).

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to 2025/2026 paper, Question One (c) in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Answer · Q1 (c) the dictionary errors, 3 marks

The dictionary defines its keys as 'name', 'age', 'city' and 'Email'. Every access then uses the wrong case, and a dictionary key is case sensitive, so each is a KeyError. Python stops at the first one it reaches:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "person.py", line 4, in <module>
    print("Name:", person['Name'])
KeyError: 'Name'

The full list of faults, so you earn every mark:

  • person['Name'], person['Age'], person['City']: the keys are lower case. Three KeyErrors.
  • person['email'] on line 7 and del person['email'] on line 11: the key is 'Email' with a capital E.
  • person['Age'] = "35" does not raise, but it creates a new key 'Age' beside the real 'age', rather than updating the age. A silent logic error.

Corrected so the case matches throughout, this is what it prints:

person.py, corrected
person = {"name": "John Doe", "age": 30,
          "city": "New York", "Email": "john.doe@example.com"}
print("Name:", person["name"])
print("Age:", person["age"])
print("City:", person["city"])
print("Email:", person["Email"])
person["age"] = "35"
person["phone"] = "123-456-7890"
del person["Email"]
print("Updated Person Dictionary:")
print(person)
Name: John Doe
Age: 30
City: New York
Email: john.doe@example.com
Updated Person Dictionary:
{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': '35', 'city': 'New York', 'phone': '123-456-7890'}

Note the final dictionary: 'age' is now the string '35', 'phone' was added, and 'Email' was deleted. That is del from Module Three doing its job.

Answer · Q1 (d) BMI, 3.5 marks

H^2 in the question is H ** 2 in Python: ** is the power operator from Module Two, not ^, which is something else entirely. Read the two values, compute, then classify with if/elif.

bmi.py
weight = float(input("Weight (kg): "))
height = float(input("Height (m): "))

bmi = weight / height ** 2

if bmi < 18.5:
    category = "Underweight"
elif bmi < 25:

elif bmi < 30:

The elif ladder needs no upper bound on each rung: by the time you reach elif bmi < 25, the first if has already ruled out everything below 18.5, so < 25 alone means the 18.5 to 25 band. That is the whole economy of elif.

Answer · Q2 (a) count-controlled loop, 3.5 marks

A count-controlled loop runs a known, fixed number of times, once per item in a sequence. In Python it is the for loop with range. You use it when you know how many passes you need before the loop starts.

for i in range(5):
    print(i)

It contrasts with a condition-controlled loop (while), which runs an unknown number of times, until a condition turns false. Count-controlled: "do this five times". Condition-controlled: "do this until the user types done".

Answer · Q2 (b) control structures, 4.5 marks

There are three kinds of control structure, and the answer names all three with an example each:

  • Sequence: statements run top to bottom, in order. The default. a = 2; b = 3; print(a + b)
  • Selection: a choice, with if/elif/else. if score >= 50: print("Pass")
  • Repetition: doing something many times, with for or while. for i in range(3): print(i)

The difference is what decides the flow: sequence has no decision, selection runs a block or skips it once, repetition runs a block again and again.

Answer · Q2 (d) the control-structures program, 6.5 marks

Six tasks in one program. Take them in order: a password loop, a validated score, a grade, a multiplication table, then a running sum. Each is a control structure from Module Three.

system.py
# i. password loop
while True:
    pw = input("Password: ")
    if pw == "admin123":
        print("Access Granted")
        break
    print("Access Denied")

# ii and iii. read a score and validate it
score = int(input("Score: "))
if score < 0 or score > 100:
    print("Error: score must be between 0 and 100")
else:
    # iv. grade it
    if score >= 70:
        print("Grade A")
    elif score >= 60:
        print("Grade B")
    elif score >= 50:
        print("Grade C")
    elif score >= 45:
        print("Grade D")
    else:
        print("Grade F")

# v. multiplication table 1 to 12
num = int(input("Number: "))
for i in range(1, 13):
    print(f"{num} x {i} = {num * i}")

# vi. sum until 0
total = 0
count = 0
while True:
    n = int(input("Number (0 to stop): "))
    if n == 0:
        break
    total += n
    count += 1
print("Sum:", total)
print("Count:", count)

The two while True loops are the two loop patterns from Module Three, Unit Two: one broken by a right password, one by a sentinel of 0.

Answer · Q4 (a) strings are immutable

Immutable means a string cannot be changed after it is made. Trying to change one character is an error:

>>> s = "cat"
>>> s[0] = "b"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

The reason: every method that "changes" a string, like upper() or replace(), actually returns a new string and leaves the original untouched. To "edit" a string you build a new one and reassign it: s = s.replace("c", "b"). A list, by contrast, is mutable and does allow list[0] = "b".

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cursor = conn.cursor()

                  (StudentID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, StudentName TEXT,
                   Class TEXT, Score REAL)""")

           (102, "Mary Johnson", "SS2", 85),

conn.commit()

print("All students:")

for row in cursor.fetchall():

        score = input("Score: ")

# ii. 5 more, "a" keeps the first ten

    for i in range(5):

        matric = input("Matric No: ")
        dept = input("Department: ")
        score = input("Score: ")

    for i, line in enumerate(f):
        if i >= 5:

def display_achievement_summary(user_name, actual_total, target_total):
    print(f"--- Progress Report for {user_name} ---")
    print("Total Steps:", actual_total)

Three value-returning functions, each handing a value back, and math.pi for the area of the circle. This is the modular style the question demands.

flooring.py
import math

def get_data():
    radius = float(input("Enter room radius (meters): "))
    price = float(input("Enter flooring price per square meter: "))
    labor = float(input("Enter labor fee: "))
    return radius, price, labor

def calculate_area(radius):
    return math.pi * radius ** 2

def calculate_total(area, material_price, labor_fee):
    return area * material_price + labor_fee

radius, price, labor = get_data()
area = calculate_area(radius)
total_cost = calculate_total(area, price, labor)

print("--- Project Estimate ---")
print(f"Total Calculated Cost: {total_cost:.2f}")
if total_cost > 10000:
    print("Status: Requires Senior Management Approval.")
else:
    print("Status: Approval not required.")

--- Project Estimate ---
Total Calculated Cost: 10547.79
Status: Requires Senior Management Approval.

The question sheet prints the sample cost as 10546.90. Run the arithmetic it asks for and you get 10547.79. The paper is wrong by 0.89, and it is worth seeing why, because the method is sound and only the printed figure is off.

>>> import math
>>> area = math.pi * 12 ** 2
>>> area
452.3893421169302
>>> area * 20 + 1500
10547.786842338604

Rounded to two places that is 10547.79. There is no radius, price or fee near the sheet's own sample that reaches 10546.90 with math.pi. Write the working, show the run, and state your figure. A marker who has run it will credit the correct number; one who has not still sees a fully justified method. This is the same discipline the whole book is built on: trust the run, not the printout, even when the printout is the examiner's.

That one table answers more marks on this paper than any other single thing in this book. Copy it out by hand until you can draw it blank.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Python is an interpreted, high-level, general-purpose programming language, known for readable syntax and dynamic typing.
  • Dynamically typed means the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so a variable may be rebound to a value of a different type and no declaration is needed.
  • Lists are ordered means every item has a position, that position is fixed until you change it, and items can be reached and sliced by that position.
  • Strings are immutable means a string object cannot be altered after it is created. Every string operation returns a NEW string, and s[0] = "X" raises TypeError. To change a string you rebind the name.
  • Sets are unique means a set holds at most one copy of any value, so adding a value already present changes nothing and len() does not grow.
  • A KeyError is raised when a dictionary is asked for a key it does not hold. d.get(key) returns None instead of raising.
  • A function is a named block of code that runs when it is called, takes parameters and may return a value. It is the unit of reuse.
  • Modularising a program gives reuse, independent testing, readability, easier maintenance, and division of work across a team. It does not make the program run faster.
  • An exception is an error detected while the program runs. try and except let the program handle it instead of stopping.
  • A module is a file of Python code that can be imported; a package is a directory of modules.

1. First five minutes: read the whole paper. Mark every question you can already do. That is not wasted time, it is the difference between answering the questions you know and running out of time before you reach them.
  2. Do the objective section first, at pace. Roughly 45 seconds a question. Any one you cannot settle in that time gets a mark in the margin and your best guess now, because there is no negative marking and a blank scores nothing.
  3. Then the long question you marked as easiest. Confidence is worth real marks, and an early complete answer stops you spending the whole paper on your worst topic.
  4. Watch the marks, not the question numbers. A part worth 2 marks wants two sentences. A part worth 8.5 wants a whole program. Writing an essay for 2 marks is how people run out of time.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
The examiner cannot run your program, so what earns the marks is that it is readable and obviously correct. Five habits do most of that work.

  • Indent visibly. Four clear spaces, or a ruled line down the block. An examiner who cannot see which lines are inside the loop cannot give you the loop mark.
  • Write the colons. Every if, for, while, def and except ends its header with a colon, and it is the most commonly dropped character under time pressure.
  • Name things properly. total, count, student_name. A program full of a, b and c reads as a guess even when it is right.
  • Convert your input. Any number read with input() gets int() or float() around it. This single line appears in almost every program this paper asks for.
  • Trace your own answer once with a small value before you move on. Three lines of a trace table in the margin catch an off-by-one that would otherwise cost the whole part.

Marks are awarded for demonstrated understanding, not for a program that would compile. A partly written answer with correct structure and clear naming scores; a blank scores nothing at all.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: the index: every one, in one place
blocks.html:
The trapWhat actually happens
Adding 5 to what input() gave youTypeError. input() returns a string; wrap it in int().
Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3It is 3.5. A single slash always gives a float. Floor division is the double slash.
Expecting numbers[1:3] to include index 3A slice stops BEFORE its stop index. range() does the same.
ys = xs.sort()ys is None. sort() changes xs and returns nothing. Use sorted(xs) for a new list.
b = a on a list, then changing ba changes too. Assignment does not copy. Use list(a) or a[:].
Looking a dictionary up by its valueKeyError. The subscript takes a KEY. Use .get() to avoid raising.
s[0] = "X" on a stringTypeError. Strings are immutable; build a new one.
Expecting "ab" * 3 to be an errorIt is "ababab". Star repeats a string; it is "ab" + 3 that raises.
A second if where elif was meantBoth blocks run. An elif chain runs at most one.
Opening an existing file with "w"It is emptied immediately. Append is "a".
Forgetting conn.commit()The rows vanish and nothing is reported.
UPDATE or DELETE with no WHEREIt applies to every row in the table.
command=run() on a buttonIt runs once, immediately, and attaches the result. Pass command=run, with no brackets.
Forgetting mainloop()The window appears and disappears at once.
Expecting int(3.9) to be 4It is 3. int() truncates; round() rounds.
A recursion with no base caseRecursionError. Every recursion needs a stopping condition and a step towards it.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Without looking: what does each of these return, and does it change what it was called on? sorted(xs), xs.sort(), s.upper(), xs.append(3), d.get("k"), cur.fetchone().
blocks.answer: sorted(xs) returns a new list, xs unchanged. xs.sort() returns None, xs sorted. s.upper() returns a new string, s unchanged, because strings are immutable. xs.append(3) returns None, xs one item longer. d.get("k") returns the value or None, d unchanged. cur.fetchone() returns the next row as a tuple, or None when they run out.
